title: Australia, New Zealand and South Africa
description: Three southern hemisphere countries, three very different stories of climate and style.
L: Barossa, McLaren Vale and the Riverland
Explain the importance of old vines

South Australia makes about half of Australia's premium wine. The Barossa Valley, settled by Silesian Lutherans in the 1840s, is famous for rich Shiraz, Grenache and Mourvèdre. McLaren Vale, south of Adelaide, is warm but cooled by the Gulf St Vincent, with Shiraz and Grenache. Inland irrigated areas like the Riverland make large volumes.

Phylloxera never reached South Australia, thanks to strict quarantine. So the Barossa has some of the world's oldest producing vines, some planted in the 1840s. Its Old Vine Charter classifies Old Vines at 35 years, Survivor at 70, Centenarian at 100 and Ancestor at 125. Old vines give low yields and concentrated fruit.
Why does the Barossa have vines over 150 years old?
South Australia's quarantine rules have kept phylloxera away, so old ungrafted vines survive.

Australia uses Geographical Indications: zones, regions and sub-regions. Labels need 85% from a named GI, grape or vintage. Blends list grapes in order of proportion, like Shiraz Cabernet. Large brands often use the broad South Eastern Australia GI, which allows blending across states.
85% rule; South Eastern Australia for blends
Match each Barossa term to its minimum vine age.
The Barossa Old Vine Charter grades vineyards by age.
South Australia's Barossa and McLaren Vale make rich Shiraz and Grenache
Quarantine kept phylloxera out, leaving very old vines
Labels follow an 85% rule; big brands use South Eastern Australia
Explain why Riesling thrives in Clare and Eden
Describe Margaret River, Yarra and Tasmania

Not all of Australia is hot. Eden Valley and Clare Valley, at higher altitude, make dry, lime-scented Riesling. Coonawarra's red terra rossa soil over limestone gives elegant Cabernet. Adelaide Hills, at up to 700 m, makes Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay. Margaret River, on the Indian Ocean, makes Bordeaux-style blends and Chardonnay.
Altitude and ocean cool the south

Victoria's Yarra Valley, near Melbourne, makes Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine. Mornington Peninsula, surrounded by sea, does the same. Tasmania, Australia's coolest state, has become the country's leading source of traditional method sparkling wine and fine Pinot Noir. The Hunter Valley, in New South Wales, makes unique Sémillon.
Which Australian regions are known for cool-climate wines?
The Riverland is hot, irrigated and high-volume.
Clare and Eden Valley Riesling sealed with screw caps since 2000 has shown how well these wines age. Ten-year-old bottles show toast and lime without losing freshness.
Which region is famous for Cabernet Sauvignon on red terra rossa soil?
Coonawarra's terra rossa over limestone gives elegant, minty Cabernet.
Clare and Eden Valley make dry Riesling
Coonawarra and Margaret River make fine Cabernet
Yarra, Mornington and Tasmania lead in cool Pinot and sparkling
Describe Hawke's Bay and Gimblett Gravels

New Zealand's two islands stretch from about 36 to 46 degrees south, and no vineyard is far from the sea. The climate is cool and maritime, with high sunlight and strong ultraviolet levels. Rain can come at harvest, so site and vintage matter. Sauvignon Blanc is over 60% of production.

Hawke's Bay, on the North Island's east coast, is New Zealand's second largest region and one of its warmest. Gimblett Gravels, an old riverbed of stony soils, stores heat and drains well. It makes Bordeaux blends and Syrah. Chardonnay is also important.
Gimblett Gravels: Bordeaux blends and Syrah
What makes Gimblett Gravels good for red grapes?
Stony soils that store heat and drain well
Old riverbed gravel stores warmth and drains, helping red grapes ripen.

Martinborough, in the Wairarapa near Wellington, is small, dry and windy. In the 1980s, scientists identified its climate and soils as similar to Burgundy's. Its Pinot Noir is concentrated and savoury. Strong winds lower yields but keep grapes healthy.
Sauvignon Blanc makes up over 60% of New Zealand's production.
Yes. It dominates exports, though Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are growing.
New Zealand is cool, maritime and bright
Hawke's Bay's Gimblett Gravels makes Bordeaux blends and Syrah

Marlborough, at the north-east of the South Island, makes about 75% of New Zealand's wine. Long, sunny days and cold nights give Sauvignon Blanc its intense passion fruit and gooseberry with high acidity. The Wairau Valley is the heart; the Awatere Valley, cooler and higher, gives more herbal styles. Montana planted the first vines in 1973.
Sunny days, cold nights, Sauvignon Blanc

Central Otago, around 45 degrees south, is the world's southernmost major wine region. It is New Zealand's only continental climate: hot, dry summers, cold winters, frost risk. Vineyards at up to 400 m, on schist and gravel, make Pinot Noir with vivid fruit and fresh acidity. Bannockburn and Gibbston are key sub-regions.
Match each region to its signature.
The South Island has two very different strengths.

Marlborough is maritime and broad, with large-scale production. Central Otago is inland, continental and small, with mostly boutique producers. Both depend on high sunlight and cool nights. Frost fans and helicopters are used in both to protect vines on cold spring nights.
Maritime and large; continental and small
Marlborough, not Central Otago, makes most of New Zealand's wine.
Marlborough makes about 75% of New Zealand's wine, mostly Sauvignon Blanc
Central Otago is continental and focused on Pinot Noir
Both rely on bright sun and cool nights
Explain the Wine of Origin scheme

South Africa's wine regions lie in the Western Cape, at about 34 degrees south. The climate is Mediterranean. The cold Benguela Current and the Cape Doctor, a strong south-easterly wind, cool the vineyards and keep them healthy. The soils are among the world's oldest: granite, sandstone and shale.
Benguela Current and the Cape Doctor

Stellenbosch, near Cape Town, is the historic heart, known for Cabernet Sauvignon and blends. Paarl and Franschhoek are warmer, with Huguenot history. Swartland, to the north, is dry, with old bush vines of Chenin Blanc, Syrah and Grenache. Elgin, Walker Bay and Constantia are cool and coastal. Constantia's sweet wine was famous in the 18th century.
The Cape Doctor blows from the south-east, cooling vines and blowing away disease.

The Wine of Origin scheme, since 1973, defines regions, districts and wards. Wines are certified with a seal on the bottle. A named grape, vintage or origin requires 85%. Producers can also make single-vineyard wines from registered sites.
Match each district to its feature.
The Cape's districts vary with distance from the sea.
The Benguela Current and Cape Doctor cool the Western Cape
Stellenbosch, Swartland and Constantia are key districts
Wine of Origin certifies origin, grape and vintage

Pinotage was created in 1925 by Professor Abraham Perold at Stellenbosch University, crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsault, which was then called Hermitage. It gives dark, red-fruited wines, sometimes with smoky or banana notes. Some modern versions are lighter and fresher; others are oaked and rich. It is South Africa's own grape.

South Africa has more Chenin Blanc than any other country, about 17,000 hectares. Once used for bulk and brandy, it now makes fine dry whites from old bush vines, especially in Swartland, Stellenbosch and Paarl. Styles range from fresh and unoaked to rich and barrel-fermented. The Old Vine Project certifies vineyards over 35 years old.
Pinotage is a cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault.
Yes. Cinsault was called Hermitage in South Africa, which explains the name Pinotage.
Look for the Certified Heritage Vineyards seal on South African labels. It shows the wine comes from a registered vineyard over 35 years old.
Which country grows the most Chenin Blanc?
South Africa has more Chenin than France, its homeland.
Pinotage, created in 1925, is South Africa's own grape
South Africa grows the most Chenin Blanc in the world
Old vines are certified and drive quality

Why does South Australia have very old ungrafted vines?

Strict quarantine has kept phylloxera out.
Which cool influences shape South Africa's Cape?
The Cape has a Mediterranean climate with dry summers, not monsoons.
Central Otago has a maritime climate.
Not true. It's New Zealand's only continental region.

Australia ranges from hot Barossa to cool Tasmania
New Zealand is maritime, except continental Central Otago
South Africa is cooled by ocean winds, with Chenin and Pinotage as signatures
Old vines matter in all three countries
